The resort booking closed at midnight, and Gurleen was sure she already knew the answer. A two-day trek, tents, a bonfire: she'd have loved it, so surely everyone would. Nilesh was ready to pay the deposit.
"Give me one hour," she said. She sent the team a short anonymous poll with three options and a line: "Tell me honestly, nothing is decided." Then she walked over to Farah and Dinesh, who rarely spoke up in meetings, and asked them directly.
By eleven the results were in. Only four of fourteen wanted the trek. Two had small children, one had a bad knee, and several simply wanted to be home by night. Gurleen laughed at herself. "I'd have booked a trip for me and three others."
They chose the day trip to the lake. Nilesh paid the deposit at 11:40.

qa.q: How many of the fourteen wanted the trek?
qa.a: Only four of fourteen.

qa.q: What did Gurleen feel when the poll results came in?
qa.a: She was amused rather than defensive, realising she'd imagined everyone wanted what she wanted, and she treated the surprise as useful.

qa.q: Which of Gurleen's steps worked best, and why?
qa.a: The anonymous poll plus asking Farah and Dinesh directly, because quieter people and those with reasons like children or a bad knee got heard.

qa.q: How might Farah feel being asked directly?
qa.a: Farah might feel noticed and more willing to say what suits them, having rarely spoken up in meetings.

grounding: It shows a woman under a deadline checking what her team actually wants, seeking out quieter colleagues, and learning from the surprise.

passage:
Alka had run the tiny momo counter in a Guwahati market for three months, and she made the chutney the way she loved it: fiery, with bhut jolokia. "Everyone likes it hot," Bhupen said, stirring the pot. "You and me both."
But Alka had noticed some plates coming back half-full. On Saturday she stuck a small card on the counter: "Too spicy? Not spicy enough? Tell me!" She also asked the college students, the office workers and an old couple who came every Sunday, not just the regulars who were her friends.
The old couple said the chutney made them cough. Two students wanted a milder sauce for dipping.
"Huh," Alka said, surprised, then pleased. "We've been cooking for the two of us."
The next week there were two bowls on the counter, one red, one pale green.

qa.q: What did Alka's card on the counter say?
qa.a: "Too spicy? Not spicy enough? Tell me!"

qa.q: Why was Alka surprised, then pleased, by the answers?
qa.a: She'd assumed most people liked the chutney as hot as she did, and the answers showed her something she could fix to serve more people. 😊

qa.q: Why was it smart of Alka to ask the old couple and the students, not only her friends?
qa.a: Her friends share her taste, so only people unlike her could show who the chutney was putting off.

qa.q: How does the change affect the old couple who come every Sunday?
qa.a: They now have a milder option and can enjoy their momos without coughing, and may feel their visits matter.

grounding: It shows a woman checking what customers actually think, asking people unlike herself, and treating the surprise as a chance to learn.

passage:
"Wait, you're for the vendor ban on MG Road?" Afreen put her chai down. "I thought everyone our age was against it."
Zubin shrugged. "Not everyone."
"Okay. I'm surprised, which probably means I only talk to people who think like me. Tell me why."
"You really want to know, or you want to argue?"
"Want to know. I'll argue later." She grinned.
"My bike shop is on that road. Customers can't park, an ambulance got stuck there last month, and the shops pay rent the vendors don't."
"Hm. I didn't think about the ambulance."
"And you?"
"The vendors are families. Some have been there thirty years."
"That's fair too."
Afreen tapped her phone. "Would you come with me to ask a couple of the vendors? And I'll come and ask your neighbours."
"Deal. Ammi will think we've gone mad, agreeing to listen."

qa.q: Where is Zubin's bike shop?
qa.a: On that road, MG Road, where the vendor ban is planned.

qa.q: What does Afreen think her surprise tells her?
qa.a: She thinks it probably means she only talks to people who think like her, so she treats it as a reason to ask rather than argue.

qa.q: What plan do Afreen and Zubin make, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: To ask a couple of the vendors and Zubin's neighbours together, so both of them hear directly from people on each side.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel when Afreen asks to understand instead of arguing?
qa.a: Zubin might feel respected and more open to Afreen's side, which shows when Zubin calls her point about the vendors fair.

grounding: It shows a woman who, surprised by her sibling's view, asks what they think and plans to hear people unlike herself.

passage:
Last spring I was put in charge of the new night-shift break room at our call centre in Mohali. I'm Revathi, the first woman shift lead there, and I was sure I knew what people wanted: a quiet room, soft lights, a shelf of books, herbal tea. That's what I'd want.
Before ordering, I made myself do two things. I sent a three-question form to all sixty people on nights. And I sat for two evenings with the people least like me: Naveen and Suraj from the billing floor, who are loud, play cricket on their phones and have never, I think, touched herbal tea.
The replies surprised me. Most people wanted a microwave, a carrom board and a phone-charging strip. Books came last. My first feeling was a little hurt, honestly. Then I thought: if it surprises me, I've learned something.
We got the microwave and the carrom board. The room is never empty now.

qa.q: How many people on nights did Revathi send the form to?
qa.a: All sixty people on nights.

qa.q: What did Revathi feel when the replies came in, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt a little hurt that her idea came last, then treated the surprise as a sign she had learned something about her colleagues.

qa.q: Which choice made the break room work?
qa.a: Checking what people actually wanted with the form and by sitting with colleagues unlike her, instead of ordering what she herself would enjoy.

qa.q: How might Naveen and Suraj experience the new break room?
qa.a: Naveen and Suraj probably feel noticed and welcome, since they were asked, and the room now has the carrom board and microwave people like them wanted.

grounding: It shows a mature person checking what others actually think, seeking out people unlike herself, and treating surprise at disagreement as a chance to learn.

passage:
Operations manager's note, March (Anand)
Disha, 24, took over the packing team leader role last month. Her first big decision was which two days the team would work from the warehouse office.
She told me she assumed everyone wanted Mondays and Fridays at home, as she does. She didn't act on that. She spoke to each of the fourteen people, including the older supervisors on the loading dock whom she rarely works with.
The answers surprised her. Most of the dock staff wanted to come in on Fridays, because that's when the trucks are loaded and questions come up. Two young parents wanted Wednesdays at home for school pickup.
When she brought me the plan, she said, "I was completely wrong about what people want, which is good to know now." She set Wednesdays and Mondays at home.
Next: I've asked her to share how she ran those conversations with the other team leads.

qa.q: How many people did Disha speak to?
qa.a: She spoke to each of the fourteen people.

qa.q: How did Disha feel about being wrong, and what shows it?
qa.a: She seemed calm and even glad, saying she was completely wrong about what people want, "which is good to know now".

qa.q: Which step in Disha's approach helped most, and why?
qa.a: Talking to the loading-dock supervisors she rarely works with, because their need to be in on truck-loading Fridays was exactly what her own assumption had missed.

qa.q: How might the two young parents feel about the final plan?
qa.a: They are likely relieved and grateful, since Wednesdays at home fit their school pickups and someone actually asked them.

grounding: It shows a mature person checking what others actually think, reaching out to those unlike herself, and treating surprise as a sign to learn.
